extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, reviewers, and readers of observational epidemiology studies (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional)
extracted.subtask_description: Checklist-style guidance for what to include when writing up observational epidemiological studies (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional). Focuses on transparent, complete reporting of title/abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, and funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 1: Title and abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Indicate the study's design with a commonly used term in the title or the abstract; (b) Provide in the abstract an informative and balanced summary of what was done and what was found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the study design explicitly in title/abstract and give an informative, balanced summary of methods and results. Use the checklist together with the STROBE explanation and elaboration article for examples. This helps readers quickly identify the design and key findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 2: Background/rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the scientific background and rationale for the investigation being reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sufficient context so readers understand why the study was done and what gap or question it addresses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 3: Objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: State specific objectives, including any prespecified hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about primary and secondary objectives and any hypotheses specified before analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 4: Study design
rubrics_metrics.description: Present key elements of study design early in the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe whether the study is cohort, case-control, or cross-sectional and key features (prospective/retrospective, population-based, etc.) early so readers can interpret methods and results in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 5: Setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the setting, locations, and relevant dates, including periods of recruitment, exposure, follow-up, and data collection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide place(s) and time(s) for recruitment and data collection, including calendar dates and duration of follow-up where applicable, to assess applicability and temporal context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 6: Participants
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Cohort study: Give the eligibility criteria, and the sources and methods of selection of participants. Describe methods of follow-up. Case-control study: Give the eligibility criteria, and the sources and methods of case ascertainment and control selection. Give the rationale for the choice of cases and controls. Cross sectional study: Give the eligibility criteria, and the sources and methods of selection of participants. (b) Cohort study: For matched studies, give matching criteria and number of exposed and unexposed. Case-control study: For matched studies, give matching criteria and the number of controls per case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report who was eligible, how participants/cases/controls were identified and recruited, reasons for including particular groups, and methods used to follow-up participants. For matched designs, state matching criteria and numbers. Where applicable provide separate information for cases and controls or exposed and unexposed groups (see asterisk note).

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 7: Variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly define all outcomes, exposures, predictors, potential confounders, and effect modifiers. Give diagnostic criteria, if applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide precise definitions and diagnostic criteria so outcomes/exposures/confounders are reproducible and interpretable; include coding, categorizations, and definitions of derived variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 8: Data sources/measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: For each variable of interest, give sources of data and details of methods of assessment (measurement). Describe comparability of assessment methods if there is more than one group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe instruments, questionnaires, laboratory methods, and measurement protocols; if multiple groups were assessed differently, describe comparability and efforts to standardise or calibrate measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 9: Bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe any efforts to address potential sources of bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State anticipated biases (selection, information, confounding, etc.) and measures taken to reduce or assess them (e.g., blinding, validation, sensitivity analyses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 10: Study size
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how the study size was arrived at.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report sample size considerations, power calculations, or rationale (feasibility, available data). Explain any decisions that affected the number of participants analysed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 11: Quantitative variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how quantitative variables were handled in the analyses. If applicable, describe which groupings were chosen and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe continuous versus categorical handling, transformations, cut-points, and reasoning for grouping to allow assessment of potential information loss or bias from categorisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 12: Statistical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Describe all statistical methods, including those used to control for confounding; (b) Describe any methods used to examine subgroups and interactions; (c) Explain how missing data were addressed; (d) Cohort study: If applicable, explain how loss to follow-up was addressed. Case-control study: If applicable, explain how matching of cases and controls was addressed. Cross sectional study: If applicable, describe analytical methods taking account of sampling strategy; (e) Describe any sensitivity analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide full detail of analytic approach so results can be interpreted and reproduced: models used, variable selection, adjustment sets, interaction tests, handling of missingness, weighting or sampling adjustments, and sensitivity analyses to test robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 13: Participants (results)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Report numbers of individuals at each stage of study—e.g. numbers potentially eligible, examined for eligibility, confirmed eligible, included in the study, completing follow-up, and analysed; (b) Give reasons for non-participation at each stage; (c) Consider use of a flow diagram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give counts and attrition at each stage (screened, eligible, enrolled, followed, analysed) and reasons for exclusion or loss, preferably with a flow diagram to clarify participant flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 14: Descriptive data
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Give characteristics of study participants (eg demographic, clinical, social) and information on exposures and potential confounders; (b) Indicate number of participants with missing data for each variable of interest; (c) Cohort study: Summarise follow-up time (eg average and total amount).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide baseline tables showing participant characteristics and distribution of exposures/confounders; report missingness for key variables and summary measures of follow-up time for cohort studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 15: Outcome data
rubrics_metrics.description: Cohort study: Report numbers of outcome events or summary measures over time. Case-control study: Report numbers in each exposure category, or summary measures of exposure. Cross sectional study: Report numbers of outcome events or summary measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present outcome event counts, incidence rates, or relevant summary statistics appropriate to the design so readers can see raw outcome data and effect magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 16: Main results
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Report the numbers of individuals at each stage of the study—eg numbers potentially eligible, examined for eligibility, confirmed eligible, included in the study, completing follow-up, and analysed; (b) Give reasons for non-participation at each stage; (c) Consider use of a flow diagram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the checklist text here repeats participant flow guidance, the intention for main results is to report primary analyses clearly (unadjusted and adjusted estimates, measures of precision, and clarity about which confounders were controlled for); present results so the main findings are interpretable. Use flow diagrams where helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 17: Other analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Report other analyses done—eg analyses of subgroups and interactions, and sensitivity analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe exploratory and prespecified secondary analyses, subgroup and interaction tests, and sensitivity analyses; state whether such analyses were prespecified and interpret cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 18: Key results
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarise key results with reference to study objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin the discussion by restating main findings in relation to the stated objectives, emphasising the most important results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 19: Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss limitations of the study, taking into account sources of potential bias or imprecision. Discuss both direction and magnitude of any potential bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about study weaknesses, possible biases, measurement error, imprecision, and how these might influence results (direction and size). This improves transparency and aids critical appraisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 20: Interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a cautious overall interpretation of results considering objectives, limitations, multiplicity of analyses, results from similar studies, and other relevant evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place findings in context of prior evidence, discuss consistency/inconsistency, avoid overstating conclusions, and acknowledge multiple analyses or potential chance findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 21: Generalisability
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss the generalisability (external validity) of the study results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider to which populations, settings, or times the results are applicable and limitations to extrapolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 22: Funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Give the source of funding and the role of the funders for the present study and, if applicable, for the original study on which the present article is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report funding sources and describe the funders' role (if any) in study design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, and reporting to disclose potential conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design-specific and asterisk notes (meta-criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eighteen items are common to all three designs, while four (items 6, 12, 14, and 15) are design-specific, with different versions for all or part of the item. For some items (indicated by asterisks), information should be given separately for cases and controls in case-control studies, or exposed and unexposed groups in cohort and cross sectional studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the checklist version tailored to cohort, case-control, or cross-sectional studies available on the STROBE website. Where asterisks indicate, present information separately by group (cases vs controls, exposed vs unexposed). The checklist should be used alongside the STROBE explanation & elaboration article for methodological background and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usage guidance and limitations of STROBE
rubrics_metrics.description: The intention is solely to provide guidance on how to report observational research well: these recommendations are not prescriptions for designing or conducting studies. The checklist is not an instrument to evaluate the quality of observational research. The checklist items should be addressed in sufficient detail and with clarity somewhere in an article, but the order and format depend on author preferences, journal style, and research field traditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: STROBE aims to improve reporting transparency rather than standardise format or assess study quality. Authors should not be 'STROBEd' rigidly; narrative elements may complement essential information. Use the checklist to assist authors, support editors and reviewers, and help readers appraise articles. Consult the companion explanation & elaboration article and the STROBE website for extensions (e.g., STREGA) and design-specific checklists.
